planting.note: Plant one-year crowns in trenches enriched with well-rotted manure as soon as soil can be worked; this early all-male Dutch hybrid was one of the pioneering supermale-derived lines bred for uniform, seedling-free beds.

directions: Franklim was bred in the Netherlands from a supermale line derived from self-pollinated 'Ruhm von Braunschweig,' making it one of the earliest all-male asparagus hybrids widely grown in Europe. Because every plant is male, beds put no energy into seed production and never develop the volunteer seedling problem common to older open-pollinated strains, so spear production stays concentrated and beds keep a tidy, even stand for years. Spears emerge thick, straight, and closely spaced along the crown, tolerating both traditional green cropping and mounded cultivation for blanched white spears. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil and avoid cutting for the first two years so crowns can build the reserves needed for a long productive life.

planting.note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil; this Yorkshire-raised cultivar is grown specifically for stalks that stay deep red in the flesh, not just the skin.

directions: Cawood Delight is a modern English rhubarb, raised in Yorkshire and selected for stout, glossy, deep red stalks colored through to the flesh rather than only on the skin, giving pies and sauces a rich color without added dye. Stalks are noticeably thick for a garden cultivar, and the plant holds its color and firmness well into the main season rather than fading to green. It is a sturdy, cold-hardy grower well suited to northern gardens but can struggle through prolonged summer heat, so give it a site with some afternoon shade in warmer regions. Harvest by pulling stalks from the outside of the crown once established, and always discard the toxic leaves.

planting.note: Plant crowns in early spring while dormant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil; this classic Dutch cultivar is a heavy, reliable early producer widely grown for forcing and general garden use across Europe.

directions: Zwolle Seedling is a long-established Dutch rhubarb valued for its heavy early flush of thick, bright red-pink stalks and its tolerance of forcing under a pot or dark cover for an extra-early crop. Compared with slower-establishing cultivars it comes into full production quickly, making it a favorite where growers want an early, dependable harvest without a long wait after planting. Flavor is well balanced between tart and sweet, with tender flesh that cooks down smoothly. As with all rhubarb, satisfy its winter chilling requirement for strong spring growth, harvest by pulling rather than cutting, and never eat the leaves, which are toxic.

common_name: Plein Blanc Inerme Cardoon (French Spineless White Cardoon)

planting.note: Start indoors six to eight weeks before last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; this old French cultivar is prized as a nearly thornless cardoon that makes blanching the stalks far less of a chore.

directions: Plein Blanc Inerme is a traditional French cardoon selected for broad, fleshy leaf ribs that carry almost no spines, unlike most cardoon strains whose sharp-edged leaves make harvest and blanching an unpleasant task. Plants form an imposing architectural clump of long, deeply cut, silvery-gray foliage a yard or more tall and wide before the ribs are ready to bundle and blanch in autumn. Wrap the outer leaves around the stalks and cover with cardboard, straw, or black plastic for several weeks before harvest to sweeten the ribs and reduce bitterness. Give it deep, rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture through the growing season for the tenderest stalks.

common_name: Violet de Provence Artichoke (Small French Purple Artichoke)
scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Violet de Provence'

planting.note: Transplant after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this nineteenth-century Provençal heirloom is grown for small, tender buds traditionally eaten whole, raw or braised, while young.

directions: Violet de Provence is a classic French heirloom prized for its slender, pointed buds flushed deep violet-purple over green bracts, picked small and young before any fibrous choke develops so the whole bud can be trimmed and eaten. It produces earlier and more heavily than many of the large-headed globe types, throwing numerous side shoots that extend the harvest over several weeks. Cutting the entire plant back hard after the first flush encourages a second smaller crop of buds within a couple of months. It is a true perennial in mild-winter climates but needs a thick mulch or overwinter protection anywhere winter temperatures drop much below the mid-teens Fahrenheit.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Gros Vert de Laon Artichoke (Large French Green Artichoke)
scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Gros Vert de Laon'

planting.note: Transplant after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this hardy old French cultivar, sometimes called 'cat head' for its rounded shape, produces very large heads on a vigorous, architectural plant.

directions: Gros Vert de Laon is a hardy French heirloom grown for its very large, rounded, tightly scaled green heads with fleshy, delicately flavored bracts, produced on a bold, silvery-leaved plant substantial enough to anchor a bed on its own. It is somewhat more cold-tolerant than many Mediterranean artichoke cultivars, a legacy of its long cultivation in the cooler climate of northern France. Cut the terminal bud while still firm and tightly closed for the best eating quality, which encourages the plant to push out smaller side buds afterward. Divide and replant offsets every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous and productive.
